unitTitle.value: Option c) AI Driven Interactive Narratives

unitDescription.value: In this unit, students explore the integration of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) to design and develop a sophisticated text-based adventure game. They apply design thinking to generate and prototype user experiences that leverage dynamic AI-generated content. They represent their solution logic through detailed flowcharts and pseudocode, which are then implemented using an object-oriented programming language. Throughout the development phase, students validate their algorithms and use specific test cases to ensure narrative consistency and technical robustness. Finally, students critique the digital footprint and ethical implications of generative AI, evaluating their projects against design criteria that consider enterprise opportunities and the future impact of automated content generation in a global context.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: The Years 9–10 cohort consists of a diverse group of boys with a wide range of digital competencies, from students with strong technical skills and personal interest in IT, to those who require further support to confidently engage with digital systems. Many students come from regional or rural backgrounds, where access to structured digital learning opportunities may have been limited. The program is designed to build on prior knowledge while introducing more advanced and applied skills relevant to future study and employment. The curriculum supports the school’s priority to equip students with transferable digital skills, critical thinking abilities, and an understanding of ethical technology use in a rapidly changing world.

description.value: Students follow a full development lifecycle to create an interactive text-based adventure game that leverages generative AI APIs for dynamic storytelling. They decompose complex problems into user stories and design prototypes that prioritise user experience before implementing their solution using modular, object-oriented programming techniques. The project concludes with a multimodal evaluation where students validate their data handling processes and critique the ethical implications and enterprise opportunities of their AI-driven system.

conditions.value:
• 4–6 weeks of class time with opportunities for supervised and independent development.
• Project Portfolio (Digital): 8–10 A4 pages or equivalent digital media.
• Submission components: Decomposed user stories, design criteria, algorithmic designs (flowcharts and pseudocode), modular source code (object-oriented), and data validation/test cases.
• Multimodal Evaluation: 2–3 minute recorded demonstration and critique, or 800–1000 words of written analytical text.
• Resources: Access to an integrated development environment (IDE), generative AI APIs, and digital design tools.
• Authentication: Teacher observation of progressive development and verification of original code through school-approved plagiarism and AI-usage protocols.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students explore the historical trajectory of interactive fiction, from early text-based adventures to modern systems enhanced by generative Artificial Intelligence. They investigate how LLMs (Large Language Models) provide a leap in immersion through procedurally generated descriptions and dynamic dialogue compared to traditional static scripts. Through guided analysis, students examine the technical architecture of AI-driven systems, identifying how local applications manage and control access to remote intelligence via Application Programming Interfaces (APIs).

resources.value: Classic IF examples (Zork, Colossal Cave Adventure), OpenAI/Anthropic API documentation, Postman or similar API testing tool, classroom presentations on API architecture.

theory.value: Explicit teaching focuses on the evolution of digital storytelling and the specific role of generative AI in creating unpredictable, high-fidelity narrative environments. Students learn about the client-server model and the function of an API as a bridge between their game logic and a large language model. The curriculum covers how digital systems manage data exchange through structured formats and the importance of secure access protocols, such as API keys and authentication headers, to control interactions with cloud-based services.

prac.value: Students participate in a comparative play-testing session, evaluating the differences in agency and immersion between classic text games like Zork and modern AI-driven narratives. They perform a 'trace' of data flow in an existing web-based AI tool to understand how a user prompt is processed and returned. Practical exercises include setting up a development environment capable of making web requests and documenting the technical constraints and rate limits specified in current AI provider documentation.

assessment.value: Formative: Completion of a technical comparison report identifying the advantages and limitations of AI-generated content versus hard-coded branching paths.

outlineTheme.value: Students explore the evolution of text-based adventure games and investigate how generative AI can enhance user immersion through dynamic dialogue and environmental descriptions. They analyse existing AI-driven systems to identify how digital systems manage and control access to large language models via APIs.

activities.title: Defining Narrative Terms
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define technical concepts using the 'Define-Example-Non-Example' model. Explain: 'Interactive Fiction' (User-led narrative, e.g., Zork), 'Large Language Model' (Predictive probability, not cognition), and 'Latency' (The technical cost of cloud processing). Model how to match a complex definition to its precise term, emphasizing precision in terminology for technical reports.
activities.studentsDo: Read the provided definitions and correctly match them to the technical terms in their workbook. Cross-reference definitions with the scaffolding provided on the board or in notes.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the vocabulary table below. Match each technical term to its correct, rigorous definition from the bank provided.
activities.questioning:
question: How does a Large Language Model differ from a static flowchart script used in early interactive fiction?
expected: A flowchart is a pre-determined decision tree where all paths are hard-coded; an LLM generates novel text responses based on statistical probability, allowing for non-linear, unpredictable narrative trajectories.
question: Why is 'Latency' a critical metric when evaluating an API-based narrative game?
expected: High latency breaks user immersion; if the narrative response time is too slow, the 'conversation' feels disjointed and unnatural, failing to simulate a responsive story environment.
activities.scaffolding: Interactive Fiction: Software that allows user input to alter the narrative progression. Large Language Model (LLM): A deep learning architecture trained on vast datasets to predict and generate human-like text sequences. Latency: The time interval between a user submitting a prompt and the API returning a generated response.
activities.eLearning: Project the vocabulary table template on the board for collective checking. Ensure students identify the distinction between 'static' scripts and 'dynamic' model-generated content.
activities.transition: Transition students to the historical analysis by framing these definitions as the foundational 'rules of the game' for the text adventures they are about to evaluate.

activities.title: History of Text Adventures
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the evolution of Interactive Fiction (IF) by contrasting the 'parser-based' systems of the 1970s with modern LLM-integrated narratives. Model the distinction between static branching logic—where every outcome is hard-coded—and dynamic generation. Example: 'In Zork, if you type 'go north' and the path isn't coded, the system returns an error. In an AI-driven system, the model generates a description of the surroundings based on the context.'
activities.studentsDo: Engage with the lecture content and complete the cloze passage to synthesize understanding of narrative architecture evolution.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill the gaps in the following paragraph using the provided word bank. Ensure terms are used in the correct grammatical context.
activities.questioning:
question: What distinguishes the branching architecture of classic IF from generative AI narratives?
expected: Classic IF is limited to pre-defined paths and static outcomes, whereas generative AI can produce unique, conversational, and context-aware responses.
question: Why is 'parser-based' input considered restrictive compared to natural language processing?
expected: Parsers require specific verb-noun syntax, whereas natural language processing allows for varied, human-like phrasing, increasing user immersion.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions for reference: Parser (software that analyses syntax), Branching Architecture (a tree-like structure of pre-defined choices), Latency (time delay in processing), Immersion (the state of being deeply engaged in a simulation).
activities.eLearning: Display the provided YouTube search results to illustrate the concept of interactive choice systems.
activities.transition: Transition students to the practical API investigation by discussing how the 'input' they just studied is actually transmitted to remote servers.

workbookSpec.title: The Evolution of IF Architecture
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the passage regarding the technological shift in interactive fiction.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. Parser, 2. Branching, 3. Deterministic, 4. Generative, 5. Latency
workbookSpec.text: Early text adventures relied on a {{1}} to interpret player commands, requiring strict syntax. The narrative design utilised a {{2}} structure, ensuring a strictly {{3}} experience where every possible path was pre-authored. In contrast, modern systems utilise {{4}} AI to create dynamic responses. Developers must now balance narrative complexity against the {{5}} introduced by API communication over network connections.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1: Parser (The interface component responsible for command syntax). 2: Branching (The narrative tree structure). 3: Deterministic (The nature of having fixed, predictable outcomes). 4: Generative (Referring to LLM capability). 5: Latency (Network delay).

activities.title: Static vs. Dynamic Comparison
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly demonstrate the contrasting architectural models: (1) Hard-coded static branching, displaying a flowchart where 'Door = Open -> Die' is a fixed logic gate. (2) Dynamic LLM generation, demonstrating how an LLM processes the prompt 'I check for rust on the hinges before opening' to generate a context-aware outcome. Highlight that static systems guarantee predictability, while AI systems trade predictability for narrative fidelity.
activities.studentsDo: Identify and categorise distinct attributes of classic text-adventure narrative structures versus modern AI-driven interactive fiction using the provided overlap table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Categorise the features of traditional narrative systems and AI-generated narrative systems. Identify shared characteristics in the overlap column. Use the comparison categories provided in the scaffolding to guide your classification.
activities.questioning:
question: Why do traditional text adventures provide higher consistency than LLM-driven narratives?
expected: Traditional systems rely on manually authored decision trees (hard-coded paths) ensuring every outcome is verified, whereas LLMs generate text based on probabilistic tokens, introducing potential inconsistencies or 'hallucinations'.
question: What is the primary trade-off when implementing an AI-driven engine over a static script?
expected: The trade-off is between narrative control/reliability and player agency/immersion. AI offers infinite interaction potential at the cost of strict narrative path enforcement.
activities.scaffolding:
Comparison Categories:
- Flexibility: Ability to handle unforeseen player inputs.
- Reliability: Certainty of outcome (100% vs probabilistic).
- Development Complexity: Authoring time (writing manual trees vs prompt engineering).
- Immersion: Degree of situational description and responsiveness.
activities.eLearning: None required. Use classroom whiteboard for final synthesis.
activities.transition: Transition to concluding the lesson by summarising the trade-offs between static logic and generative AI in game design.

workbookSpec.title: Interactive Fiction: Static vs. Dynamic Models
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate the architectural differences between Traditional Text Adventure (Left) and AI-Driven Interactive Fiction (Right). Place shared traits in the overlapping centre column.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Left Only: Fixed logic gates, predictable outcomes, limited vocabulary support, high development time for branching. Right Only: Probabilistic generation, context-aware descriptions, handles natural language, potential for hallucination. Both: Player agency, goal-oriented gameplay, text-based output, core game loop architecture.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Traditional Only: Requires manual authoring for every branch, outcome is binary/fixed, memory efficient. AI Only: High compute cost, requires API connection, infinite narrative possibilities, unpredictable outputs. Both: User input processing, core game state management, narrative progression through text, require clear prompt/command structures.

culminate.summarise: Recap: We moved from rigid branching to dynamic generation. Next lesson explores the 'pipes' (APIs) behind this.

activities.title: API Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explain the API as a waiter: the 'client' (user application) sends a request (order) via the waiter (API) to the kitchen (server). To get service, the client must present an 'API Key'—like a diner's membership card—which is verified against an Authentication Header. Model a standard HTTP request on the whiteboard, highlighting: 'POST /v1/chat/completions', 'Authorization: Bearer sk-123...', and the JSON body.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the matching exercise to identify API components, then provide clear, technical definitions for architectural concepts used in game-to-AI communication.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Match the three key API components using the provided definition bank. 2. Define the three architectural concepts in the second section of the table.
activities.questioning:
question: Why do we use an API Key in a professional development environment?
expected: To manage rate limits, ensure billing accuracy, and secure the endpoint against unauthorised access.
question: What happens if our Authentication Header is missing or malformed during a request?
expected: The server will return a 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden error, preventing data exchange.
activities.scaffolding: Endpoint: The specific URL destination where an API accepts requests. API Key: A unique secret token assigned to a user/application for authentication and tracking. Authentication Header: Metadata passed in the request that confirms the requester's identity.
activities.eLearning: Use the projector to display a live Postman request or a raw cURL command snippet demonstrating how the header, key, and endpoint are structured within a real API call.
activities.transition: Transition to investigating the actual data flow in a browser network tab to see these terms in action.

workbookSpec.title: API Architectural Components
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the matching and definition tasks below.
bank: A specific URL destination where an API accepts requests.
A unique secret token assigned to a user for authentication.
Metadata passed in the request that confirms identity.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Endpoint: The specific URL destination where an API accepts requests. API Key: A unique secret token assigned to a user/application for authentication and tracking. Auth Header: Metadata passed in the request that confirms the requester's identity. Client-Server: An architecture where the client requests data/services and the server provides the response. Rate Limit: A constraint on how many requests a client can make to an API within a timeframe. JSON Format: A lightweight, text-based format for data exchange between systems.

activities.title: Client-Server Architecture
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the Request-Response cycle using the St Brendan's College network as an analogy. Use a diagram to explain: 1. User Input (Client), 2. JSON Serialization (Client), 3. API Call/Authentication (Network), 4. LLM Processing (Server), 5. Deserialization (Client). Explicitly explain why APIs are necessary: they provide a secure bridge for the game to request intelligence without exposing the game's full codebase to the LLM.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the 'API Request Journey' flow diagram. Identify the specific moments where data format changes (e.g., from raw text to JSON).
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the data flow diagram below to map how your game client talks to an AI model. Use the provided stages to fill in the blanks.
activities.questioning:
question: Why must the game client convert raw player input into a JSON format before sending it?
expected: The API server requires a structured, standardised format to interpret the data reliably, rather than unstructured natural language.
question: What is the function of an API key in this request flow?
expected: It acts as authentication to verify that the client has permission to access the server and helps the provider track usage limits.
question: What happens if the API request returns a 404 or 500 error?
expected: The game client would be unable to update the interface, necessitating error-handling logic to inform the user.
activities.scaffolding: Definition of JSON: JavaScript Object Notation, a lightweight data-interchange format. Definition of Request-Response: A communication protocol where a client sends a request and a server returns a response. The stages provided for the flow are: User Input, JSON Serialization, API Request, LLM Processing, JSON Deserialization, UI Update.
activities.eLearning: Project the interactive diagram on the board. Provide students with the workbook link to complete their own flow mapping.
activities.transition: Transition to the practical assessment of API documentation where students will find the actual endpoint URLs for their chosen model.

workbookSpec.title: API Request Lifecycle
workbookSpec.prompt: Map the journey of a player's request from game input to AI-generated narrative response.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. Player types input -> 2. Client encodes input as JSON payload -> 3. POST request sent to API endpoint -> 4. LLM generates completion -> 5. Response parsed back into game text.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. User Input (Fixed). 2. JSON Serialization (Student Fill). 3. Secure API Request (Student Fill). 4. LLM Inference (Student Fill). 5. JSON Deserialization (Student Fill). 6. Display to Player (Fixed). Branching: Successful authentication leads to processing; failed authentication leads to a specific error state returned to the UI.

activities.title: Analyzing API Constraints
activities.teacherDoes: Display the OpenAI API documentation page on the main projector. Demonstrate how to locate the 'Rate Limits' section using the search function. Model how to extract a specific constraint value—for instance, noting that a free-tier account may be limited to 3 requests per minute compared to higher tiers. Explain that these technical boundaries are essential for maintaining the stability and economic viability of cloud-based AI services.
activities.studentsDo: Access the provider documentation via the browser. Identify the specific limits outlined for the 'Tier 1' or free-tier usage models. Complete the 3-2-1 exit ticket regarding API constraints, focusing on the trade-offs between system availability and model performance.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using the provided API documentation, complete the 3-2-1 exit ticket. Identify three technical constraints, two methods for managing costs, and one primary concern regarding latency.
activities.questioning: How might rate limits impact the user experience in a real-time game application? Expected: The game might freeze or fail to generate a response during high-traffic periods. Why is token management crucial for developers? Expected: To prevent excessive costs and avoid exceeding the model's context window, which could lead to truncated or nonsensical responses.
activities.scaffolding: Common Constraints: 1. Rate Limits (RPM: Requests Per Minute, RPD: Requests Per Day). 2. Latency (TTFT: Time To First Token). 3. Token Limits (Context window size and cost per 1k tokens). 4. Authentication (API Key validity).
activities.eLearning: Browser access to OpenAI or Anthropic API documentation. Use digital split-screen view: documentation on one side, workbook on the other.
activities.transition: Conclude the session by summarizing how these technical constraints act as the 'walls' within which your game logic must operate.

sections.label: 3: Identify three technical constraints defined in the documentation
2: List two methods developers use to manage API costs or performance
1: State one primary reason why latency affects game immersion

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 3: (Answers may include) Rate Limits (e.g., requests per minute), Token Limits (input/output context length), and Latency (the delay between request and response). 2: (Answers may include) Caching frequently requested data to avoid repeat API calls, and monitoring token usage to ensure it stays within a defined budget. 1: (Answers may include) High latency breaks the 'suspension of disbelief'; players expect immediate feedback in dialogue systems; long delays make the AI feel 'robotic' or disconnected from the game world.

activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the mechanics of an HTTP request within the browser environment. Model the process of opening Developer Tools (F12), selecting the 'Network' tab, and filtering for 'Fetch/XHR' traffic. Explicitly point to the headers (authentication tokens) and the request payload (the prompt data) to show how data is structured before it leaves the client. activities.questioning:
question: Why is the 'Network' tab the primary tool for auditing API interactions?
expected: It allows for the inspection of raw data transit between client and server, including headers, payloads, and response status codes.
question: How do status codes, such as 200 or 401, indicate the outcome of a request?
expected: A 200 code indicates a successful connection and processing; a 401 indicates an authorisation failure, often due to an invalid or missing API key.
activities.scaffolding: Core Terms: 1. Request Header: Metadata containing authorisation tokens or content format. 2. Request Payload: The specific data (prompt) sent to the server. 3. Response: The data returned by the server (AI completion). 4. Status Code: A numeric indicator of whether the request succeeded (200) or failed (4xx/5xx).

workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1: Request Headers (Metadata); 2: Request Payload (Input data); 3: Response Status (Success/Error); 4: Response Body (Returned Data)

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. Request Header: Contains the API key (Authorisation) and Content-Type definition. 2. Request Payload: The JSON formatted text query sent to the LLM. 3. Response Status (200 OK): Signals the request was successfully received and processed. 4. Response Body: The raw text completion or JSON object returned by the server containing the AI-generated response.

activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the use of browser developer tools (Network tab) to observe API traffic. Model how to filter for XHR/Fetch requests while interacting with the Livingstorne Shire Council website search feature, explicitly pointing out the Request Headers and Payload. Provide an example: 'When I type into the search bar, the browser creates a JSON payload containing my query string; observe how the server responds with a 200 OK status.'

Why might the API response return a JSON object rather than a raw HTML snippet? 1. API Endpoint: The specific URL where an API receives requests. 
2. JSON Payload: The data sent in the body of an HTTP request or response.

activities.teacherDoes: Distribute the workbook. Demonstrate a 'latency scenario' where a request is sent to an API and a delay is introduced. Explain that developers must manage these delays to maintain narrative flow. Model a response: 'High latency interrupts the pacing of text-based games, as players lose engagement if the system pauses mid-sentence to wait for data retrieval.'

activities.visibleInstructions: Using the provided structure, analyse the impact of high latency on AI narrative systems and propose mitigation strategies.
activities.questioning:
question: What happens to the user experience if the game logic continues executing while waiting for an API response?
expected: The game state may become desynchronised, or the UI may freeze, resulting in a loss of narrative continuity.
question: Why is 'streaming' a common solution in LLM applications?
expected: Streaming allows the user to see the text generating in real-time, masking the latency and improving the perception of responsiveness.
activities.scaffolding: Latency: The time delay between a user input and the system output. Strategies: Asynchronous requests (sending requests in the background), streaming responses (showing text word-by-word), or implementing 'thinking' animations to occupy the user.

workbookSpec.title: Technical Constraints: Analysing Latency
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate the relationship between API response time and player immersion.

sections.label: 1. Explain: How does latency specifically break the 'flow' of a narrative?
2. Propose: Suggest two technical UI strategies to manage user expectations during a high-latency response.
3. Conclude: Why must API rate limits be documented before system deployment?

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. Latency breaks 'flow' by removing the immediate feedback loop required for interactive fiction. If the game pauses, the player is reminded of the computational engine, shattering immersion. 2. Strategies: Implementing loading spinners or 'typing' indicators (UX); using streaming tokens to display text as it arrives (technical). 3. Documentation is required to prevent 'rate limiting' errors, where the API service blocks requests, crashing the game experience for the end-user.

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students apply design thinking principles to define the scope and narrative direction of their interactive game. They use divergent thinking techniques to generate unique story worlds and character concepts, ensuring they cater to a diverse audience with varying gameplay preferences. By interviewing peers, students practice gathering requirements and translating them into formal user stories that drive the development process. They apply problem decomposition to break their narrative vision into modular components such as the 'World Engine,' 'NPC Manager,' and 'User Interface.'

resources.value: Design thinking templates, Miro or Canva for mind mapping, user story guides, interview protocols for stakeholder feedback.

theory.value: The theory component introduces design thinking as a structured approach to solving complex digital problems. Students learn the 'Define' and 'Ideate' phases, focusing on how to transform broad ideas into specific, actionable user stories (As a [user], I want [feature], so that [benefit]). Lessons cover the importance of decomposition in software engineering, explaining how breaking a project into smaller, manageable subsystems facilitates more efficient coding and debugging. Students also explore how to design for diverse audiences by considering accessibility and varied player motivations.

prac.value: Students engage in rapid brainstorming sessions, using mind mapping and 'Crazy 8s' to generate narrative hooks and game mechanics. They conduct structured interviews with classmates to identify player needs, which are then documented as formal user stories and design criteria. Using collaborative digital tools, students create a decomposition diagram that maps out the primary functional requirements of their game, including a project scope that identifies 'must-have' vs 'could-have' features for their MVP (Minimum Viable Product).

assessment.value: Formative: Peer-to-peer feedback on drafted user stories and a teacher review of the project decomposition diagram and scope document.

outlineTheme.value: Students apply design thinking by using divergent techniques to generate ideas for their interactive narrative and interviewing peers to develop detailed user stories. They decompose their game concept into manageable components, identifying the specific needs of a diverse audience and defining the project’s scope.

activities.title: Design Thinking Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the Design Thinking process using the 5-stage framework (Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test). Model the connection between these stages and game development: 'Define' is about establishing the 'User Story', while 'Ideate' is where we perform divergent thinking to expand on game mechanics. Provide a brief example: 'Empathise' involves interviewing peers about their gaming habits before building a single line of code.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the workbook table by matching the correct design phase to its corresponding definition from the provided word bank. Review the definitions to ensure an understanding of the logical flow from research to evaluation.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Review the Design Thinking Phase terms in your workbook. 2. Select the accurate definition from the provided bank and write it in the Match column next to the correct term.
activities.questioning:
question: Why might a developer start with 'Empathise' rather than jumping straight to 'Prototype'?
expected: To ensure the solution solves a genuine user need or pain point rather than assuming features that might not be engaging or functional.
question: How does 'Define' differ operationally from 'Ideate'?
expected: Define focuses on narrowing the scope and articulating the core problem statement, whereas Ideate is a divergent process of brainstorming as many solutions as possible without immediate judgement.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions for reference: 1. Empathise: Conducting research to understand audience requirements and motivations. 2. Define: Stating the core project problem and specific scope. 3. Ideate: Divergent brainstorming of narrative hooks and mechanics. 4. Prototype: Developing a simplified or interactive model for testing. 5. Test: Gathering user feedback to refine the game design.
activities.eLearning: Students are to remain focused on the provided definitions in their workbook; avoid the use of external generative AI tools or web searches for this foundational vocabulary activity.
activities.transition: We have established the framework; now we apply the 'Ideate' phase using rapid brainstorming techniques to generate our narrative hooks.

activities.title: Ideation: Crazy 8s
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the Crazy 8s technique: explain that we are prioritising volume over perfection to break cognitive blocks. Model a rapid idea generation scenario: 'Scenario: A lost diver near the Keppel Bay Marina needs to guide an AI drone back to the surface.' Sketch 8 quick stick-figure storyboards on the board to demonstrate that 'rough' is acceptable. Instruct students to focus on rapid narrative beats.
activities.studentsDo: Read the cloze notes to frame the design thinking context, then use the provided grid to sketch 8 unique AI narrative hooks within the 8-minute timeframe.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Complete the guided notes below to understand the purpose of Ideation. 2. Use the grid in your workbook to sketch 8 distinct narrative concepts for your AI game. Focus on variety, not detail.
activities.questioning:
question: Why does the Crazy 8s method prioritise quantity over quality?
expected: It lowers the barrier to entry, encourages risk-taking, and prevents designers from becoming overly attached to the first concept.
question: How does divergent thinking assist in solving complex digital problems?
expected: It expands the solution space, ensuring a wider variety of potential narratives or mechanics are considered before narrowing down to a final design.
activities.scaffolding: Divergent Thinking: A process of generating creative ideas by exploring many possible solutions. Ideation: The creative process of generating, developing, and communicating new ideas. Crazy 8s: A design sprint method to sketch 8 distinct ideas in 8 minutes.
activities.eLearning: Use the YouTube search term 'call to action website convert visitors' to briefly discuss how narrative elements (like those in their sketches) can guide user engagement on platforms like the Capricorn Coast Visitor Information site.
activities.transition: Now that we have 8 distinct narrative seeds, we will select the most promising concept and begin formalising it into a user story.

workbookSpec.title: Ideation Principles
workbookSpec.prompt: Fill in the missing terms to complete the definition of Ideation.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. divergent; 2. fixation; 3. narrative hook; 4. motivation
workbookSpec.text: The Ideation phase relies on {{1}} thinking, which focuses on quantity over quality. By using the Crazy 8s method, designers avoid {{2}}, which is when you get stuck on the first idea you have. A successful {{3}} for an AI game should consider the user's {{4}} and what keeps them engaged in the story.

activities.workbookMaterials: Crazy 8s Sketch Grid and Ideation Notes
activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. divergent (focuses on breadth of ideas); 2. fixation (prevents early commitment to mediocre ideas); 3. narrative hook (the initial interest-grabber); 4. motivation (the player's internal drive to progress).

activities.title: Narrative Concept Refinement
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that in professional game design, a narrative must be concise enough to communicate to developers and stakeholders. Model the transformation of a vague idea into a defined hook using the 'Who, What, Conflict' framework: 'A space-scavenger (Who) must repurpose ancient technology (What) to survive an encroaching solar storm (Conflict).'
activities.studentsDo: Select their strongest Crazy 8s concept and draft a narrative summary that explicitly states the protagonist, the inciting action, and the core conflict. They must then identify two distinct user characteristics that this narrative appeals to.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Review your Crazy 8s ideation from the previous activity. 2. Write your narrative summary below, ensuring you address the 'Who, What, and Conflict' framework. 3. List two target audience characteristics that make this narrative engaging for different player types.
activities.questioning:
question: How does your core conflict provide a clear 'problem' for the player to solve?
expected: The conflict creates a sense of urgency or goal-orientation, forcing the player to make choices that impact the outcome.
question: Why is it important to define specific player characteristics at this early stage?
expected: Defining characteristics ensures that the narrative mechanics align with player motivations, such as strategic depth for thinkers or immersion for casual players.
activities.scaffolding: Who (Protagonist): The central figure interacting with the world. What (Action): The primary task or loop. Conflict: The challenge or obstacle preventing easy success. Example: 'A disgraced knight (Who) must rebuild a fallen village (What) while bandits constantly raid for supplies (Conflict).'
activities.eLearning: Check student concepts for feasibility; ensure the 'Conflict' is something that can be translated into AI-driven dialogue or branching narrative decisions rather than purely visual action.
activities.transition: Now that the concept is refined, we will validate these assumptions by interviewing peers to gather genuine stakeholder feedback.

lessons.title: Requirement Gathering & User Stories
lessons.learningGoal: Construct formal user stories by translating stakeholder interview feedback.

orientate.smartStart: Recall: What is the primary difference between a 'Functional Requirement' and a 'User Story'?
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can construct formal user stories by translating stakeholder interview feedback

activities.title: User Story Anatomy
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model the 'As a... I want... So that...' framework, emphasizing how this structure mitigates scope creep and ensures user-centric development. Write the following example on the board: 'As a novice player, I want a hint system, so that I don't feel discouraged when solving puzzles.' Deconstruct this sentence, identifying the persona, the functional requirement, and the underlying value proposition. Demonstrate how this specific articulation assists developers in prioritising features during the Minimum Viable Product (MVP) phase.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the modelled demonstration by annotating the provided user story diagram in their workbook. Students identify the specific components of the user story and map them to the corresponding sections of the annotation figure.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Review the provided user story example. 2. Use the numbered callouts to label the specific components: Persona, Action/Feature, and Benefit. 3. Annotate the 'So that' section to describe why this benefit is critical for the target audience.
activities.questioning:
question: What functional impact occurs if we omit the 'So that' component from our user story?
expected: The development team loses sight of the user's underlying motivation, leading to features that may lack relevance or utility.
question: Why is it essential to explicitly define the user persona before specifying the feature?
expected: Different user personas have distinct requirements; identifying the user prevents generic features that fail to address the needs of the target demographic.
activities.scaffolding:
User Story Structure: 
- [As a <user>]: The target audience/persona.
- [I want <feature>]: The specific functional requirement.
- [So that <benefit>]: The rationale or value proposition for the user.
activities.eLearning: Project a clean, high-contrast digital version of the user story template on the main display to facilitate visual alignment with the physical workbooks.
activities.transition: Having established the anatomy of a user story, we will now transition to peer-to-peer interviews to gather the stakeholder requirements necessary for drafting your own user stories.

workbookSpec.title: Deconstructing the User Story
workbookSpec.prompt: Using the provided user story figure, annotate the key structural components of the requirement.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1: As a novice player (Persona), 2: I want a hint system (Feature), 3: So that I don't get stuck on puzzles (Benefit).
workbookSpec.figureHint: Screenshot of a standard User Story template format

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Callout 1 (Persona) identifies 'novice player' as the user role. Callout 2 (Feature) identifies 'hint system' as the requested functionality. Callout 3 (Benefit) identifies 'don't get stuck on puzzles' as the value-add. The completed annotation should clearly link these three distinct grammatical segments to their roles within the requirements gathering process.

activities.title: Stakeholder Interview
activities.teacherDoes: Model the 'Interview, Filter, Formalise' workflow. Demonstrate an effective stakeholder interview by asking a student volunteer about their game idea. Explicitly demonstrate how to transform a vague need like 'I want the game to be fast' into a functional user requirement using the structure: 'As a [player], I want [feature], so that [benefit].' Provide feedback on active listening techniques during the peer pairs.
activities.studentsDo: In pairs, alternate roles as interviewer and stakeholder. Use the Interview Table to document the narrative concept, primary gameplay motivations, and potential pain points. Following the interview, transcribe the raw feedback into the provided User Story drafting table.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Pair with a partner. 2. Interview them using the provided prompts, recording their requirements in the Interview Table. 3. Synthesize their needs into a draft User Story using the Agile template provided.
activities.questioning: How does framing a requirement as a user story change your understanding of the developer's scope? Expected: It shifts the focus from 'what the game does' to 'what value the user experiences'. Why is it critical to identify pain points during the interview phase? Expected: To proactively design against frustration points and improve overall game usability.
activities.scaffolding: User Story Template: As a [type of player], I want [to perform an action], so that [I gain this specific benefit/value].
activities.eLearning: Facilitate peer discussion to ensure the Interview Table is populated with specific, actionable data rather than generic game features.
activities.transition: Conclude interviews. Transition to the drafting stage where individual needs are synthesised into formal User Stories for the project scope.

activities.title: Drafting User Stories
activities.teacherDoes: Model the refinement process by converting vague interview feedback into formal syntax. Example: If a peer says 'I want the game to look cool,' model rewriting it: 'As a player, I want high-contrast visual themes, so that I can easily navigate menus even if I have visual impairments.' Circulate and verify that 'So that' clauses focus on specific project benefits rather than vague outcomes.
activities.studentsDo: Synthesize interview notes into three formal user stories using the specified framework. Students must ensure each story represents a distinct requirement identified during the stakeholder interview phase.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Review your peer's interview notes from the previous task. 2. Identify three key features. 3. Draft one user story for each feature using the format: As a [persona], I want [action/feature], so that [value/benefit]. 4. Swap with your partner to verify that your stories are testable and clearly defined.
activities.questioning:
question: How does framing your requirement as a 'So that' statement help you prioritise features for an MVP?
expected: It forces us to define the specific value proposition, which highlights which features are essential (must-have) versus merely decorative (could-have).
question: If a user story is too broad, such as 'As a player, I want the game to be fun,' why does this fail as a requirement?
expected: It is not actionable or testable. A developer cannot verify 'fun,' but they can verify specific mechanics like 'scoring systems' or 'levels'.
activities.scaffolding: User Story Framework: 1. Persona (Who is the user? e.g., Beginner Player, Expert Gamer). 2. Action (What do they need to do? e.g., Save progress, Adjust difficulty). 3. Benefit (Why do they need this? e.g., To avoid losing data, To increase challenge). Ensure your stories follow the format: As a [User], I want [Feature], so that [Benefit].
activities.eLearning: Use the 'call to action website buttons convert visitors' YouTube resource to consider how button placement and user flows (as discussed in the video) might inform your UI-based user stories.
activities.transition: Now that we have established these user requirements, we will decompose these features into functional modules to begin system architecture.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Assessment Checklist: 1. Persona identified? (e.g., Casual Player). 2. Action concrete? (e.g., Change audio settings). 3. Benefit provides value? (e.g., To customise the experience for accessibility). Ensure no stories are 'I want the game to be fast' (too vague); ensure they are functional requirements (e.g., 'I want a sprint mechanic, so that I can traverse the map quickly').

lessons.title: Project Decomposition & Scope
lessons.learningGoal: Decompose an interactive narrative project into modular components and define the Minimum Viable Product (MVP).

orientate.smartStart: Quick fire: What does MVP stand for? Why does it matter in software development?
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can decompose an interactive narrative project into modular components and define the Minimum Viable Product (MVP)

activities.title: System Decomposition Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the necessity of standardized terminology in systems analysis. Model the definition of Decomposition using the analogy of a modular car engine, where each part serves a distinct function that can be repaired independently. Clarify that MVP (Minimum Viable Product) acts as the project anchor to prevent uncontrolled expansion. Explain that precision in vocabulary is essential for team communication in a professional development environment.
activities.studentsDo: Students complete the terminology matching exercise in the workbook. They compare their understanding against the provided definitions to ensure they can articulate the core concepts of software architecture before starting their design diagrams.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Review the definition bank provided below the table. 2. Write the correct definition index (or letter) next to the corresponding term in the table. 3. Ensure your definitions align with the project scoping focus.
activities.questioning:
question: How does identifying an MVP mitigate the risk of project failure?
expected: By focusing resources only on essential features, it ensures the core functionality is delivered on time and provides a working foundation, thereby preventing feature bloat.
question: Why is it necessary for a developer to define the World Engine separately from the NPC Manager?
expected: To reduce code coupling; allowing developers to update AI dialogue logic without breaking the game's core save, load, or inventory functionality.
question: What is the primary indicator that a project is suffering from scope creep?
expected: The continuous addition of features not originally included in the MVP, resulting in missed deadlines and budget overruns.
activities.scaffolding: Decomposition: The process of breaking a complex problem into smaller, manageable subsystems. MVP: The version of a product with just enough features to be usable by early customers. World Engine: The core architecture managing narrative state, environment, and rules. NPC Manager: The subsystem responsible for handling AI-generated dialogues and character state. Scope Creep: Uncontrolled changes or continuous growth in a project’s scope that occurs without adjustments to time, cost, and resources.
activities.eLearning: Ensure all students have accessed the unit definition sheet if they require additional support for the matching task.
activities.transition: Now that we have established the vocabulary, we will move to mapping the hierarchy of your game components.

activities.title: Feature Ranking for MVP
activities.teacherDoes: Explain the MoSCoW method (Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have) to differentiate project requirements. Model the selection of a 'Must-Have' by using an example: 'If we are building a mystery game, the 'Narrative Engine' is a Must-Have because without it, the game is non-functional, whereas 'Voice Acting' is a 'Nice-to-Have' because the game functions with text alone.' Facilitate a discussion on why scope creep often kills student projects and emphasize that an MVP must be the smallest possible version that demonstrates the core mechanic.
activities.studentsDo: Evaluate six prospective features for their interactive narrative game. Students must prioritize these features into a ranked list to form the Minimum Viable Product (MVP), considering the limitations of their project timeline.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Review the provided feature bank. 2. Rank the features from 1 (Most critical for MVP) to 6 (Least critical/Nice-to-have). 3. Write your justification for your top two 'Must-Have' selections in the space provided below.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is it dangerous to categorize all features as 'Must-Have' at the start of a project?
expected: It leads to scope creep, where the project becomes too complex to complete within the assessment timeframe, resulting in an unfinished product.
question: How does defining an MVP help the development process for an interactive narrative?
expected: It allows the developer to focus on the core narrative loop and mechanics first, ensuring the project is playable and functional before adding aesthetic or secondary features.
activities.scaffolding: Definition of MVP: The Minimum Viable Product includes only the essential features required to make the product functional and deliver value to the user. Features: AI Chat Engine (Core logic), User Login (Authentication), Save Game System (Persistence), Inventory System (Mechanics), High Score Tracker (Gamification), Background Music (Atmosphere).
activities.eLearning: Project the 'Call to Action' video on conversion buttons to illustrate how specific design choices direct user focus. Direct students to the Livingstone Shire Council website as an example of a clear, feature-focused interface.
activities.transition: Now that we have confirmed our project scope, we will translate these ranked priorities into specific user stories.

workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. AI Chat Engine, 2. Save Game System, 3. Inventory System, 4. Background Music, 5. User Login, 6. High Score Tracker

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Priority rationale: 1 (AI Chat Engine): Essential core mechanic for narrative. 2 (Save Game): Essential for user persistence. 3 (Inventory): Essential for interaction. 4 (Background Music): Enhances experience but not functional. 5 (User Login): Often non-essential for a local student game. 6 (High Score): Secondary to narrative depth.

activities.title: Defining Project Scope
activities.teacherDoes: Present the 'Minimum Viable Product' (MVP) framework, emphasizing that scope definition is the primary guardrail against project bloat. Model the process of evaluating a 'could-have' feature versus a 'must-have' feature using the St Brendan's College project criteria: 'If the project lacks this feature, does it fundamentally break the narrative experience?' Demonstrate how to verify technical dependencies like API credentials or save/load state logic.
activities.studentsDo: Evaluate their proposed game features against the checklist provided. They must categorize features as 'MVP' (must-have) or 'Stretch' (future-proofing). Students then cross-reference their checklist items against the project timeline to confirm feasibility.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Review your project decomposition list. 2. Tick each completed task or approved scope item in your workbook. 3. Sign off on your MVP feature set to confirm the project scope is fixed for the prototype phase.
activities.questioning:
question: How does defining a 'Must-Have' MVP feature set prevent scope creep in your narrative project?
expected: It creates a clear boundary, forcing us to focus on core functionality before adding 'nice-to-have' features, preventing the project from becoming too complex to finish.
question: What is the consequence of failing to secure API credentials or backend logic during the scope definition phase?
expected: It creates a project bottleneck; without these dependencies defined early, we cannot build the core interactivity, likely causing the prototype to fail or stall.
activities.scaffolding: Project Scope Categories: 1. Core Mechanics (Backend/Logic): Save/Load states, API integrations, Variable tracking. 2. User Experience (Frontend/UI): Menu navigation, Interaction buttons, Text display. 3. Narrative Architecture: Branching dialogue trees, Character state transitions, Ending triggers.
activities.eLearning: Students review the 'Call to action website buttons' YouTube search term results to understand how UI design influences user engagement, then apply those lessons to their UI feature checklist.
activities.transition: Scope is now formally locked; transition to environment setup and initial prototyping for the next session.

They focus on how the game state is managed—tracking variables like player location, inventory, and health—and how these variables interact with AI-generated outputs. A significant focus is placed on the logic of asynchronous communication, preparing students to design algorithms that handle the latency of AI API responses without interrupting the user experience.

theory.value: Explicit instruction is provided on representing algorithms using formal flowcharts and pseudocode, with a focus on decision-making branches and state-driven logic. Students learn how to model the 'Game Loop' and the integration points where AI content is injected into the predefined story structure. Theory also covers the concept of asynchronous calls (promises/callbacks) and how to design fail-safe logic in pseudocode to handle instances where an AI API might return an unexpected or malformed response, ensuring the system remains robust.

They write pseudocode for a core game module that demonstrates how user input is captured, sent to an AI for processing, and then used to update the internal game state. Students perform a 'desk check' on their classmates' logic to identify potential infinite loops or orphaned states where the player might become stuck, refining their designs based on this technical validation.

assessment.value: Formative: Technical review of the narrative flowchart and pseudocode for the primary interaction loop, assessed for logical completeness and error handling.

They design algorithms that handle asynchronous API calls and define how AI-generated content will be integrated into the predefined story structure.

lessons.title: Mapping Narrative Logic
lessons.learningGoal: Construct a flowchart that maps the 'Golden Path' and key narrative branching trajectories.

orientate.smartStart: On the whiteboard: Draw a simple decision diamond and a process rectangle. Ask: 'What is the functional difference between these two symbols in a flowchart?' (Answer: Diamond is for decision/branching; Rectangle is for process/action).
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can construct a flowchart that maps the 'Golden Path' and key narrative branching trajectories

activities.title: Flowchart Symbology Review
activities.teacherDoes: Model the standard flowchart symbols using a projector. 'Students, note that flowcharts are the architecture of your narrative logic. In QCAA digital solutions, we prioritise precise notation. If your logic is ambiguous—for example, if a Decision Diamond leads to an unlabelled path—the system fails. Let’s map the Room Entry sequence: I use an Oval for Start, a Parallelogram for the system detecting the player's key, and a Rectangle for unlocking the door. Model how a Diamond branches the logic: IF key == true THEN open ELSE deny.'
activities.studentsDo: In the workbook, match each function to its correct technical symbol from the bank. Use the provided scaffolding to ensure notation accuracy.
activities.visibleInstructions: Label the provided symbol descriptions by matching them with the technical terms in the bank. Ensure your notation aligns with standard flowchart conventions.
activities.questioning:
Why is it critical that we use a Diamond symbol specifically for player choices? Expected: Because it represents a conditional statement that forces the execution path to split based on boolean logic (True/False).
What outcome occurs if a developer fails to label the exit branches of a Decision Diamond? Expected: The process becomes logically ambiguous, leading to potential 'orphaned states' or logic errors where the system cannot determine the next state.
activities.scaffolding:
Standard Flowchart Symbols:
- Oval: Termination (Start/End)
- Rectangle: Action (System process/calculation)
- Diamond: Decision (Conditional logic/Branching)
- Parallelogram: Data Input/Output (User interaction or display)
activities.eLearning: Use the overhead projector to display a live logic-trace of a 'Room Entry' sequence to demonstrate real-time pathing.
activities.transition: Check for correct symbol usage before progressing to the complex mapping of narrative trajectories.

activities.title: Understanding Asynchronous Calls
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the 'Non-blocking Principle'. Model an analogy: Ordering at a cafe versus a takeaway counter. In synchronous logic, the kitchen stops until your coffee is done. In asynchronous, you receive a buzzer and return to your seat, allowing the kitchen to handle other orders. Explicitly define: 'Latency' as network transmission delay, 'Asynchronous' as non-sequential task execution, 'Callback' as the event-handler that triggers upon response arrival, and 'Fail-safe' as the defensive programming required to keep the system state stable if an API request times out or returns malformed data.

expected: The entire application becomes unresponsive (freezes) while waiting for an external server response, breaking immersion.

expected: A timeout function or error handler that alerts the user or loads a fallback narrative state rather than waiting indefinitely.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions for reference: 1. Latency (The time delay between sending a request and receiving a response). 2. Asynchronous (Operations that run independently without blocking the main execution thread). 3. Fail-safe (System logic designed to default to a safe state if an error occurs). 4. Callback (A function executed automatically only after an asynchronous process finishes).

keyTeachingExperiences.value: Students transition from logical design to technical implementation by establishing the object-oriented foundation of their adventure game. They participate in a collaborative modeling session to map their previous decomposition diagrams into a class hierarchy, identifying shared attributes across game entities. Explicit instruction focuses on creating modular Python classes that represent the physical and narrative state of the game world, ensuring that each component functions independently before integration. Students explore how encapsulation allows them to hide the complexity of state changes within objects, making the overall system more maintainable.

theory.value: Theory focuses on the core tenets of object-oriented programming (OOP), specifically encapsulation and abstraction within the context of game development. Students learn how to define classes for 'Locations', 'Items', and 'Characters', using constructors to initialise unique states and methods to handle interactions. The lesson covers the importance of access modifiers and the 'Single Responsibility Principle', explaining why a Room object should manage its own exits and descriptions rather than relying on a global script. This theoretical framework provides the scaffolding necessary to build a scalable engine that can handle a growing narrative without code fragility.

They practice instantiation by creating a network of linked room objects that represent the starting area of their narrative. Subsequent exercises involve creating an 'Item' class with properties such as 'weight' or 'is_hidden' and developing a method within the Room class to manage an inventory of these objects. By the end of the week, students execute a simple navigation script that allows a player object to move between instantiated room instances and query their state.

outlineTheme.value: Students begin implementing their solution using an object-oriented programming language, focusing on creating modular classes for game entities like locations, items, and characters. activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define the four key pillars of OOP in the context of game development. Use the 'Blueprint and House' analogy: A Class is the architectural drawing (blueprint), while an Instance is the actual house built from that design. Explain that Encapsulation is like the walls of the house; it hides the complex wiring and plumbing (data) from the residents, providing simple light switches (methods) to interact with them. expected: The class methods (functions) are the interface; they allow interaction without needing to know internal logic.
activities.scaffolding: Class: The structural blueprint defining attributes and methods. Instance: An individual object created from a class. keyTeachingExperiences.value: This week focuses on the technical integration of generative AI, with a heavy emphasis on secure data exchange and prompt engineering. Students investigate the mechanics of interacting with external Large Language Models (LLMs) through API requests, learning how to format data using JSON for structured communication. They participate in 'prompt-tuning' workshops, where they experiment with different system instructions to maintain narrative consistency and tone. A key focus is placed on cybersecurity, specifically the ethical and safe management of API keys and the implementation of environment variables to protect sensitive credentials in shared environments.

resources.value: OpenAI/Anthropic API documentation, Python 'dotenv' library, JSON linting tools, prompt engineering cheat sheets.

theory.value: The theory component covers the anatomy of a RESTful API request, including headers, payloads, and authentication. Students learn about the JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) format as a standard for data exchange between their local program and the cloud-based AI service. Lessons also explore advanced prompt engineering techniques, such as 'few-shot prompting' and the use of system personas to constrain AI output, ensuring the generated text fits the game’s specific genre. Additionally, students are introduced to the Australian Privacy Principles in the context of data sent to third-party AI providers.

prac.value: Students set up a secure configuration file using environment variables to store their API keys, ensuring no sensitive data is hard-coded in their main scripts. They write Python functions using the 'requests' library to send a user’s action to the AI and receive a descriptive narrative response. Practical tasks include 'cleaning' the API response to remove unwanted formatting and handling common network errors or rate-limit exceptions. Students refine their 'system prompt' to ensure the AI behaves as a consistent dungeon master, ignoring out-of-character requests from the player.

assessment.value: Formative: A 'Prompt Validation' task where students must demonstrate an API call that returns a narrative description conforming to a specific genre and length constraint.

outlineTheme.value: Students explore the technical requirements of integrating external AI services, focusing on secure API key management and structured data exchange. They practice writing and refining prompts to ensure the generative output remains consistent with the game’s tone and functional requirements.

activities.title: Defining API Anatomy
activities.teacherDoes: Present the 'Postal System' analogy for API communication. Explain: The Header acts as the envelope, carrying vital information about the package (authentication, content-type). The Payload is the package contents (the specific data being transmitted). The Endpoint is the destination postbox (the URL providing access). Model writing a clear definition by breaking down 'Endpoint' as 'The location where an API lives'.

activities.questioning: Why do APIs require headers even if they are only sending simple data? Expected: Headers provide essential metadata like authentication tokens and content-type, which the server needs to safely process the request. If you had to describe a JSON Payload as an analogy, what would it be? Expected: It is the 'letter' or the 'data parcel' being sent to the server for processing.
activities.scaffolding: Reference Table: Header (Metadata regarding request formatting and auth); Payload (The actual data being sent/received); Endpoint (The specific URL/address of the API service).

activities.questioning:
question: What happens if a developer omits a comma between key-value pairs?

JSON Structural Rules:

3. Key-value pairs are separated by a colon (:).
4. Pairs are separated by commas (,).
5. No trailing commas are permitted after the final item.

activities.title: I-Do: Security Risk Analysis
activities.teacherDoes: Display a repository on the projector with a hard-coded API key. Run a 'git diff' to show how clearly credentials stand out in version history. Explain the concept of 'Secret Sprawl'—the risk of sensitive keys leaking into public repositories like GitHub. Introduce the 'dotenv' library as the standard industry solution for environment variable management. Demonstrate the workflow: (1) Creating a .env file, (2) Adding the key, (3) Referencing it in code using os.getenv, and (4) Confirming .env is explicitly listed in .gitignore.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the demonstration on their own machine, performing an immediate security audit of their project repository using the provided checklist.
activities.visibleInstructions: Audit your project directory for security vulnerabilities. Complete every checklist item to ensure your API credentials are isolated from source code.
activities.questioning:
question: If you push your code to a public repository with an API key, why can't you just delete the commit to fix it?
expected: The key remains in the git history; a new commit does not remove the previous exposure.
question: What is the specific purpose of the .gitignore file in relation to security?
expected: It acts as a whitelist for git, preventing sensitive configuration files like .env from being tracked or pushed to remote servers.
activities.scaffolding:
Security Best Practices:
1. Hard-coded keys: Sensitive strings (e.g., sk-...) written directly in .py files.
2. .env files: Local text files that store configuration variables; these are excluded from Git.
3. .gitignore: A control file that instructs Git to ignore specific files or patterns.
4. Environment variables: Values loaded into the operating system's memory at runtime rather than stored in application code.
activities.eLearning: Demonstrate live terminal commands: 'ls -a' to locate hidden files and 'cat .gitignore' to verify exclusion rules.
activities.transition: Proceed to refactoring your existing code to use the python-dotenv library.

activities.questioning:
question: What happens if you accidentally commit your .env file to a public GitHub repository?
expected: Your API key becomes public, allowing others to use your credentials, incur costs on your account, or access your services.
question: Why do we call load_dotenv() before calling os.getenv()?
expected: load_dotenv() reads the .env file and adds its contents to the environment variables; without it, os.getenv() cannot find the key.
activities.scaffolding: 1. Terminal command: 'pip install python-dotenv'. 2. .env file content: 'API_KEY=sk-xxxx...'. 3. Accessing values: Use 'os.getenv("KEY_NAME")' which returns 'None' if the key is missing, preventing crashes.

activities.questioning:
question: Why is it insufficient to simply delete the .env file from the folder before pushing code?
expected: Deleting the file does not remove it from the Git commit history; it would still exist in past commits and remain accessible to anyone who clones the repository.
question: What is the primary risk if an API key is exposed in a public repository?
expected: Malicious actors can scrape the repository history to steal keys, leading to unauthorized usage, financial costs, and potential data breaches.
activities.scaffolding:
The .gitignore file tells Git which files or directories to ignore entirely. 

Key rules:
1. .gitignore should always be in the root directory.
2. Secrets (API keys, passwords, database URLs) belong in .env.
3. Never commit .env.

workbookSpec.title: Security Justification
workbookSpec.prompt: Document the necessity of credential isolation within your development workflow.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Storing API keys in a local .env file ensures they are never committed to version control. If committed, keys become part of the repository's history, making them accessible to anyone with clone access. Even after deletion, they remain in the git history unless specifically purged, posing a perpetual security risk.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Vulnerability: Committing an .env file embeds plain-text secrets into the version history. This history is permanent and accessible to anyone with repository access, allowing them to steal keys even if the file is later deleted. Verification steps: 1. Add .env to .gitignore. 2. Save the .gitignore file. 3. Run 'git status' in the terminal. 4. Confirm .env does not appear in the 'Untracked files' list.

activities.title: System Persona Analysis
activities.teacherDoes: Present the concept of system personas as a method to enforce narrative consistency. Model the construction of a negative constraint: 'Instead of saying "Be helpful," define the persona to say "You are an unreliable narrator; never confirm the truth of an event directly." question: Why include 'negative constraints' (e.g., 'Do not admit you are an AI') in a system prompt?
expected: To create a 'guardrail' that prevents the LLM from reverting to its default helpful/cautious assistant training, ensuring immersion remains unbroken.
question: How does 'few-shot prompting' differ from a static system prompt in maintaining a consistent tone?
expected: A static prompt provides abstract rules, while few-shot prompting provides concrete examples of the desired style and rhythm, which the AI then imitates.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions: 
- System Persona: The defined identity the AI adopts (e.g., Cynical Detective, Ancient Archivist).
- Negative Constraint: Explicit instructions on what content or behaviour to avoid (e.g., 'Never mention modern technology').
- Few-Shot Prompting: Providing examples of desired input-output pairs to calibrate the AI's response style.

Your goal is to guide players through the St Brendan's ruins. Always maintain a sombre tone. Never mention modern technology.'). activities.questioning:
question: Why is it necessary to include explicit 'Never' constraints in a system prompt?
expected: To prevent the AI from defaulting to its standard, neutral persona or introducing inappropriate/anachronistic content that breaks immersion.
question: How do 'few-shot' examples within the system prompt enhance consistency?
expected: They provide concrete templates for the desired tone and structure, reducing ambiguity and forcing the AI to mirror the provided style.
activities.scaffolding:
Use the following framework for your system prompt: 
1. ROLE: Define the AI's specific persona (e.g., 'A stoic guide'). 
2. GOAL: State the narrative objective (e.g., 'Describe the environment of the Capricorn Coast'). 
3. CONSTRAINT: Mandatory rules (e.g., 'Keep responses under 50 words'). 
4. NEGATION: What to avoid (e.g., 'Do not use emojis' or 'Do not explain that you are an AI').

Remind students to document the specific prompt iteration that achieved the desired output, as this is critical for their assessment evidence.

question: If the model hallucinated external information, which part of your prompt failed to constrain the data source?
expected: Students should identify that the prompt lacked specific boundaries (e.g., 'Only use provided lore' or 'Do not use outside knowledge').
activities.scaffolding:
Success Criteria for Narrative Integrity:
1. Persona Adherence: The AI never references its identity as an LLM/AI.
2. Length Constraint: Responses remain within the specified token limit/character count (e.g., < 150 words).

items: Narrative tone matches established genre (e.g., consistent vocabulary, mood).
Response length strictly adheres to character/word count constraints.
AI ignored all meta-requests or out-of-character 'jailbreak' attempts.

The IPO Cycle:
- Input: The raw text captured from the user keyboard.

activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the concept of 'State Management' as the architectural backbone of narrative consistency in AI-driven games. Model the definition of 'State' by using a simple game scenario: 'If a player picks up a key, the State variable 'has_key' must change from False to True.' Explain that persistent data structures, specifically History Buffers, are essential to prevent 'narrative amnesia' where an AI forgets crucial player choices. Demonstrate how to classify data components based on whether they require persistence or are ephemeral.

activities.questioning:
question: Why is a 'stateless' AI problematic for long-form narrative consistency?
expected: Without state, the AI lacks memory of past interactions, leading to hallucinations or contradictory story beats as it cannot reference player inventory or previous choices.
question: How does a 'History Buffer' improve AI output compared to standard prompt injection?
expected: It acts as a curated context window, ensuring the AI receives a structured record of relevant past events rather than relying on session-less, isolated prompts.
activities.scaffolding: State: The complete set of active variables defining the game environment at a specific time. Persistence: Data that remains saved and accessible even after a loop iteration or session ends. History Buffer: A temporary, sequential holding area for data (previous choices) waiting to be processed by the LLM context. Ephemeral Data: Temporary information, such as current turn animations or UI hover effects, that do not impact future story state.

activities.title: Defining Verification & Validation
activities.teacherDoes: Explain the distinction between verification (building the thing right - technical adherence) and validation (building the right thing - user requirement satisfaction). Define 'edge cases' as boundary condition inputs (e.g., negative integers, excessive string length, or null inputs) that challenge algorithmic limits. Model a structured test case example on the board: Test ID: TC01; Input: 'Examine Sword'; Expected Output: 'The sword is rusted and heavy.'; Actual Output: [Observation].
activities.studentsDo: Define the testing terminology provided in the workbook and complete the matching table to demonstrate conceptual understanding of software quality assurance standards.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Provide a concise definition for each testing term in the table. 2. Match the terms to the appropriate definition using the provided term bank.
activities.questioning:
question: Why might an inventory overflow represent a critical failure in game logic?
Expected: It forces the system into a state outside of its constrained variables, leading to memory allocation errors or narrative crashes.
question: If an AI generates a location reference missing from your game map, what is the consequence for validation?
Expected: Validation fails because the game state loses referential integrity, causing a 'null reference' error or a break in the narrative flow.
activities.scaffolding: Verification: The process of evaluating software to determine whether it complies with specified requirements (Building the thing right). Validation: The process of evaluating software during or at the end of the development process to determine whether it satisfies specified requirements (Building the right thing). Edge Case: A problem or situation that occurs only at an extreme operating parameter. Mock Object: A simulated object that mimics the behaviour of real components in controlled ways.
activities.eLearning: Display a summary slide contrasting Verification vs Validation. Provide links to software testing documentation via the St Brendan's College portal.
activities.transition: Transition students to test case design by instructing them to apply these definitions to their own game project's inventory and movement logic.

Expected: 'System displays error message and does not add item'. Explain that negative testing—trying to break the system—is critical for robust software.

activities.questioning:
question: Why is it critical to test boundary conditions (e.g., maximum inventory capacity) rather than just typical usage?
expected: To ensure the system doesn't crash, glitch, or allow illegal states when variable limits are reached.
question: What is the primary risk of relying on live API calls during the initial testing phase of game development?
expected: Non-deterministic results due to network latency, unexpected service interruptions, and unnecessary consumption of usage credits.

activities.title: I Do: Trace Debugging
activities.teacherDoes: Project a buggy code snippet—a common logic error where an inventory state fails to clear after a narrative transition. Execute the following steps: 1. Set a breakpoint at the point of transition. 2. Demonstrate 'Step Over' versus 'Step Into' to isolate the scope. 3. Monitor the 'Variables' pane to confirm if 'item_count' resets to zero. 4. Explicitly explain that stepping allows us to inspect the 'black box' of execution. Model thinking aloud: 'I suspect the loop is terminated prematurely because the variable condition isn't met, so I am checking the current value of the iterator here.'
activities.studentsDo: Follow the demonstration on personal screens or the main projection, identifying exactly where the logic fails to update the state variable during the simulated execution.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the debugger demonstration. Identify the line where the 'current_location' or 'inventory_count' variable fails to update correctly. Use the checklist to track the debugging procedure.
activities.questioning:
question: What does the debugger reveal about the execution environment that a standard print statement cannot?
expected: The debugger shows the persistent state of memory and all variables simultaneously, rather than just the output stream.
question: Why is 'stepping' considered a more rigorous validation method than simple trial-and-error testing?
expected: Stepping allows for precise identification of the exact line where logic deviates from the algorithmic design, rather than guessing based on game output.
activities.scaffolding: Debugging Definition: A systematic process of identifying, analysing, and removing bugs from software. Logic Error: Code that runs without crashing but produces unintended or incorrect results. Execution Flow: The path the program takes through code blocks.
activities.eLearning: Project IDE screen (VS Code or Pycharm) connected to the primary projector. Ensure the 'Watch' window and 'Call Stack' panels are clearly visible.
